categories.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
categories.blurb: JavaScript injected into a page that runs in someone else's browser.
categories.what: The application puts attacker-controlled data into a page without escaping it for the context it lands in (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL). The victim's browser runs the script as if the site itself had written it.
categories.impact: Session and token theft, actions performed as the victim, reading page data, phishing from inside the real domain. In back-office tools (blind XSS) it often becomes a staff account takeover.
where: Values reflected in the response: search, error messages, redirect parameters
Stored content: profile names, comments, file names, upload metadata (SVG, EXIF)
DOM sinks: innerHTML, document.write, location, postMessage handlers that skip origin checks
Markdown renderers, rich-text editors and link previews
test: Find the context your value lands in before choosing a payload
Try breaking out of the attribute, the tag and the JavaScript string separately
Look for sanitizer gaps: mutation XSS, uncommon tags, double encoding
Check the CSP: does it really block execution, or is there an allowed gadget or JSONP endpoint?
For blind XSS, use a payload that calls home when it fires in another system
fix: Context-aware output escaping (the framework does it; avoid the "raw" and "dangerouslySet" escape hatches)
A maintained sanitizer (DOMPurify) for HTML that must be accepted
A strict nonce-based CSP and Trusted Types as a second layer
Session cookies with HttpOnly and SameSite

categories.name: SQL & NoSQL Injection
categories.blurb: User input that changes the query sent to the database.
categories.what: The application builds queries by concatenating user-supplied text. The attacker changes the structure of the query to read, modify or delete data — and, on some databases, run commands on the server.
categories.impact: Full database disclosure, login bypass, data tampering and, depending on configuration, code execution on the server.
where: Filters, sorting and pagination (ORDER BY, LIMIT) — places prepared statements do not cover
Legacy APIs, reports, exports and internal endpoints
Headers and cookies that are logged or used in queries
JSON query operators in NoSQL stores ($ne, $gt, $where)
test: Single quotes, comments and arithmetic to see whether the response changes
Boolean and time differences when no error is visible (blind)
For NoSQL, swap values for objects and operators
Prove impact with the least data possible: database version, current user
fix: Parameterized queries everywhere; allowlists for column names and sort direction
A database user with the least privilege it can work with
Type validation on input (a number is a number, not an object)

categories.name: Code & Command Execution (RCE)
categories.blurb: The attacker gets to run code or commands on the server or client.
categories.what: Untrusted input reaches an interpreter: a shell, eval, a template engine, a deserializer or a plugin loader. Covers command injection, code injection, SSTI and insecure deserialization.
categories.impact: Control of the server, access to secrets, lateral movement into the internal network. Usually the highest severity a program pays for.
where: File and image conversion (ImageMagick, ffmpeg, LibreOffice, Ghostscript)
Templates rendered with user data (Jinja, Twig, ERB, Handlebars)
Serialized objects in cookies, queues and caches (Java, PHP, Python pickle, Ruby Marshal, YAML)
Integrations with git, ssh, tar, zip and other command-line tools
Outdated dependencies with a known CVE
test: Work out which interpreter receives the data and use the right separator for it
Use an out-of-band channel (DNS/HTTP) to confirm blind execution
In templates, start with a simple arithmetic expression
Prove impact with a harmless command (id, hostname) and stop there
fix: Never pass input to a shell; use APIs that take an argument list
Data formats that cannot execute (JSON) instead of native serialization
Sandboxed templates, and never user data as the template itself
Process isolation (containers, seccomp, an unprivileged user)

categories.name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
categories.blurb: The server makes requests wherever the attacker points it.
categories.what: A feature fetches a URL supplied by the user (webhook, import, preview). The attacker points that URL at internal services only the server can reach.
categories.impact: Reading cloud metadata and temporary credentials, reaching internal panels and APIs, scanning the network and, sometimes, RCE on unauthenticated services.
where: Webhooks, import by URL, "upload from link", remote avatars
PDF and screenshot generators, link previews
XML, SVG and document processors that resolve external references
Configurable integrations (Git server address, SMTP, proxy)
test: Point it at a server you control to confirm the request and read its headers
Try internal addresses and the cloud metadata endpoint
Get around filters: redirects, DNS rebinding, IPv6, decimal and octal notations
Try other schemes: file://, gopher://, dict://
fix: An allowlist of destinations; resolve DNS and validate the final IP
Block private and link-local ranges after following redirects
An isolated fetch service on a network with no internal access
Cloud metadata hardened against SSRF (IMDSv2 and equivalents)

categories.name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
categories.blurb: Another site triggers actions in the logged-in victim's account.
categories.what: The application accepts state-changing requests trusting only the session cookie. A page controlled by the attacker makes the victim's browser send that request.
categories.impact: Changing the email or password, altering settings, purchases, data deletion — anything the victim can do with one click.
where: Sensitive actions without a token: change email, link an account, disable 2FA
Endpoints that accept GET or a different Content-Type for the same action
Login and OAuth flows (login CSRF, missing state parameter)
JSON APIs that also accept form submissions
test: Remove the token, send it empty, or use one from another account
Switch the method and the Content-Type
Check SameSite on the session cookie and whether a subdomain can get around it
Build an HTML proof of concept and test it in a current browser
fix: A session-bound anti-CSRF token on every state-changing action
Cookies with SameSite=Lax or Strict
Origin/Referer checks as an extra layer
Re-authentication for critical actions

categories.name: IDOR — Insecure Direct Object Reference
categories.blurb: Change an identifier, get someone else's resource.
categories.what: The application uses an identifier from the client (id, UUID, file name) to fetch an object without checking that it belongs to whoever is asking.
categories.impact: Reading and changing other users' data at scale: orders, messages, documents, addresses, invoices.
where: Any parameter that looks like an identifier, including inside JSON and headers
Export, download and attachment endpoints
Mobile APIs and GraphQL (id, node and globalId arguments)
Secondary actions: edit, delete, share, invite
test: Use two accounts and swap identifiers between them
Try every verb: sometimes GET is protected and PUT or DELETE is not
Find where IDs leak (other API responses, emails, public URLs)
Change the type: an array of IDs, a numeric ID in place of a UUID, a wildcard
fix: An ownership check on the server for every object access
Queries always scoped to the session's user or organization
Automated cross-account authorization tests

categories.name: Access Control & Privilege Escalation
categories.blurb: Doing what your role should not allow.
categories.what: The rules for who can do what are not enforced consistently on the server. A regular user runs admin functions, or a limited member acts as the owner.
categories.impact: Access to admin areas, role changes, reading other organizations' data and full control of a workspace.
where: Admin functions hidden only in the interface
In-between roles (viewer, guest, billing) and invitations
Old endpoints and previous API versions
State changes: what still works after someone is removed from a team?
test: Map each role's actions and replay every request as the lowest role
Hit admin routes directly, bypassing the interface
Look for role or organization parameters the server accepts (mass assignment)
Try old tokens and sessions after the user is demoted or removed
fix: Deny by default; centralized authorization on the server
Check role and scope on every endpoint, not just the route
Invalidate sessions and tokens when a role changes

categories.name: Authentication & Sessions
categories.blurb: Flaws in login, 2FA, password recovery, OAuth and sessions.
categories.what: The mechanism that confirms who the user is has a shortcut: predictable password recovery, 2FA that can be skipped, misconfigured OAuth, sessions that never expire, or no limit on attempts.
categories.impact: Account takeover, often with no interaction from the victim.
where: Password recovery: predictable tokens, or tokens leaked through Referer or the Host header
Second factor: steps that can be skipped, codes with no attempt limit
OAuth/SSO/SAML: loose redirect_uri, missing state, account confusion through unverified email
Sessions that stay valid after a password change or logout
test: Walk each flow and try to skip steps by going straight to the final request
Measure attempt limits on login, OTP and recovery
Change the email or phone mid-flow and see who receives the code
Check what happens to sessions and tokens after a password change
fix: Random, single-use tokens with a short lifetime
Attempt limits per account and per source
Strict redirect_uri validation, plus state and PKCE
Revoke sessions on sensitive events

categories.name: Information Disclosure
categories.blurb: Data that should never have left the server.
categories.what: The application reveals sensitive data: other users' personal information, secrets in responses and forgotten files, internal details in error messages or debug endpoints.
categories.impact: Ranges widely — from a worthless version string to bulk personal data, or credentials that open other doors.
where: API responses carrying more fields than the interface shows
Exposed files: .git, backups, .env, logs, directory listings
Debug, metrics and internal documentation endpoints
JavaScript bundles and mobile apps with embedded keys
test: Compare the API's JSON with what the screen displays
Force errors and read the messages
Look for well-known framework routes (actuator, debug, server-status)
Always show what the data lets you do — that is what sets the severity
fix: Serialize only allowed fields
Generic error messages in production
Secrets out of the repository, and rotated when they leak

categories.name: Path Traversal & File Read
categories.blurb: Leaving the allowed folder to read or write server files.
categories.what: A file name or path from the user is used on the file system without normalization. With sequences like ../ the attacker reaches files outside the intended directory. Includes LFI.
categories.impact: Reading source code, configuration and keys; when writing is possible, overwriting files and executing code.
where: Downloading and viewing files by name
Zip and tar extraction (zip slip) and imports
Template, language or theme parameters that become an include
Static servers and proxies that normalize paths differently from the backend
test: ../ sequences with encoding variations (%2e%2e%2f, double encoding, backslashes)
Absolute paths and symbolic links inside archives
Normalization differences between the proxy and the application
fix: Resolve the canonical path and check it is still inside the base folder
Map identifiers to files instead of accepting names
Validate every entry when extracting archives

categories.name: Open Redirect
categories.blurb: The site sends the user to a destination the attacker chose.
categories.what: A destination parameter (next, url, return_to) is used in a redirect without validation.
categories.impact: Low on its own (phishing with a trusted domain). The value is in chaining it: stealing OAuth tokens, bypassing SSRF filters and CSP.
where: Login, logout and OAuth flows
Email links and internal link shorteners
Redirects done in JavaScript (location = parameter)
test: URL variations: //evil.com, /\evil.com, https:evil.com, @, lookalike subdomains
The javascript: scheme when the redirect happens client-side (it becomes XSS)
Combine with OAuth to capture a code or token
fix: Accept only relative paths or a list of destinations
Compare the host after parsing the URL, not by prefix

categories.name: Business Logic
categories.blurb: The system works as coded — but the rule has a hole in it.
categories.what: There is no technical payload: the attacker uses the flow in a way the developers did not anticipate. Negative values, steps out of order, limits enforced only on the client, coupons reused.
categories.impact: Financial fraud, free use of paid features, getting around limits and product rules.
where: Payments, prices, coupons, credits and refunds
Plan limits and paid features
Multi-step flows and verifications
Invitations, referrals and reward programs
test: Understand the product as a user before testing it
Change quantities, prices and currencies; try negatives, zero and huge values
Repeat, skip and reorder steps
Ask: what is the server trusting the client not to change?
fix: Validate every rule on the server
Model states and allowed transitions explicitly
Monitor for anomalous usage patterns

categories.name: Race Conditions
categories.blurb: Simultaneous requests that slip through the same check.
categories.what: The application checks a condition and then acts on it, without atomicity. Parallel requests all pass the check before any of them records its effect.
categories.impact: Coupons and balances used more than once, duplicated withdrawals, limits and 2FA bypassed, resources created beyond quota.
where: Redeeming coupons, gift cards and transfers
Limits: invitations, attempts, votes, items per plan
Email verification and data changes in the middle of a flow
test: Send the same request in parallel (the single-packet attack over HTTP/2)
Compare the final state with what a single request should produce
Look for the window between check and write in multi-step flows
fix: Atomic database operations, locks and uniqueness constraints
Idempotency keys on financial operations

categories.name: HTTP Smuggling, CRLF & Caching
categories.blurb: Protocol-level attacks: smuggling, header injection and caches.
categories.what: Proxy and server parse the same request differently, or the application lets the attacker inject line breaks and headers. Includes cache poisoning, cache deception and Host header attacks.
categories.impact: Hijacking other users' requests, bypassing proxy controls, XSS stored in the cache, poisoned password-reset links.
where: Chains of CDN, load balancer and application server
Parameters reflected into headers (Location, Set-Cookie)
Headers outside the cache key (X-Forwarded-Host and friends)
Dynamic routes the cache treats as static files
test: Content-Length versus Transfer-Encoding disagreements; HTTP/2 downgrades
Inject %0d%0a into values that come back in headers
Look for unkeyed inputs that change the cached response
On production systems, test with great care: smuggling affects other users
fix: Normalize requests at the edge and reject ambiguous ones
HTTP/2 end to end where possible
Never reflect input into headers; review the cache key

categories.name: XXE & XML Attacks
categories.blurb: The XML parser resolves external entities defined by the attacker.
categories.what: An XML parser with external entities enabled processes an attacker's document and reads local files, makes network requests or eats memory until it falls over.
categories.impact: Server file read, SSRF and denial of service.
where: Uploads of XML-based formats: SVG, DOCX, XLSX, SAML, RSS
APIs that accept XML as well as JSON (switch the Content-Type)
SOAP integrations and old importers
test: An external entity pointing at a local file or a server you control
Out-of-band exfiltration with an external DTD when nothing is returned
XInclude when you only control part of the document
fix: Disable DTDs and external entities in the parser
Prefer simpler formats where you can

categories.name: File Upload
categories.blurb: Sending a file the server should not accept or serve.
categories.what: Validation of the upload's type, content or destination falls short. The file is executed by the server, served as HTML on the application's domain, or written outside the intended folder.
categories.impact: From stored XSS (SVG, HTML) to code execution (web shell), by way of file overwrite and denial of service.
where: Avatars, attachments, data imports, media editors
What happens afterwards: resizing, antivirus, conversion
Storage buckets with a controllable pre-signed URL
test: Double extensions, upper case, null bytes and a fake Content-Type
Polyglot files and SVG with script
File names with ../ and special characters
Check which domain serves the file, and with which headers
fix: An allowlist of types validated by content
Serve uploads from a separate domain with Content-Disposition: attachment
Rename files and store them outside the web root

categories.name: Subdomain Takeover
categories.blurb: A forgotten DNS record points at a service anyone can claim.
categories.what: A DNS record (usually a CNAME) still points at a third-party resource that was removed — a bucket, a PaaS app, a status page. The attacker registers the resource and controls what the subdomain serves.
categories.impact: Phishing on a legitimate domain, theft of cookies scoped to the parent domain, bypass of CSP and of OAuth and CORS allowlists.
where: Marketing, documentation, status and test-environment subdomains
Services retired after migrations
Orphaned NS and MX records
test: Enumerate subdomains and look for the provider's "resource not found" responses
Confirm the provider lets you register the same name
Keep the proof discreet (a file at a random path) and host nothing visible
fix: Remove the DNS record before decommissioning the resource
An inventory and continuous monitoring of dangling records

categories.name: Clickjacking, Spoofing & Phishing
categories.blurb: Misleading the user about what they are seeing or clicking.
categories.what: The interface can be framed, forged or manipulated: clickjacking on sensitive actions, content and text injection, spoofed senders or address bars, homographs.
categories.impact: Unintended one-click actions and more convincing phishing. Programs usually require a real sensitive action before they accept it.
where: Pages with one-click actions and no frame protection
Messages and error pages that reflect text from the URL
Email clients, browsers and apps that display an origin or sender
test: Check X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors on sensitive pages
Build the proof around the real action, not just the frame loading
For spoofing, show the full deception scenario
fix: CSP frame-ancestors (and X-Frame-Options for older browsers)
Confirmation for critical actions
Never reflect free text into pages on the domain

categories.name: Denial of Service (DoS)
categories.blurb: A cheap request that is expensive for the server.
categories.what: A small input causes disproportionate use of CPU, memory, disk or connections: catastrophic regex, decompression, unbounded queries, loops and process crashes.
categories.impact: The service becomes unavailable for everyone or for one account. Many programs exclude volumetric DoS; they accept what is asymmetric and at the application layer.
where: Parsers: JSON, XML, YAML, images, archives
Regular expressions applied to user input (ReDoS)
Pagination and GraphQL queries with no depth limit
Unbounded fields that are stored and reprocessed
test: Measure the cost in your own environment whenever you can
Show the asymmetry with one request, without taking production down
Read the program policy first — DoS nearly always has its own rules
fix: Limits on size, depth, time and rate
Linear-time regex engines, or timeouts
Heavy work isolated in queues

refs.title: OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet

categories.name: Memory Corruption
categories.blurb: Overflows, use-after-free and out-of-bounds reads in native code.
categories.what: Memory management errors in C, C++ and similar languages: buffer overflow, use after free, out-of-bounds read or write, integer overflow, type confusion.
categories.impact: From crashes and memory disclosure to code execution. The dominant category in projects such as curl, PHP, Ruby and browsers.
where: Parsers for binary formats and protocols
Image, audio, video, font and compression libraries
Native extensions of interpreted languages
test: Fuzzing with sanitizers (ASan, UBSan, MSan) is the most productive route
Read Internet Bug Bounty reports to see the expected format
Minimize the test case and include the sanitizer stack trace
fix: Bounds and integer checks; safe APIs
Continuous fuzzing and sanitizers in CI
Memory-safe languages for new code

categories.name: Cryptography & Secrets
categories.blurb: Insecure transport, certificate validation, weak algorithms and exposed secrets.
categories.what: Sensitive data travels or rests without proper protection: poorly validated TLS, weak algorithms and modes, predictable randomness, passwords and keys in clear text or baked into the code.
categories.impact: Intercepted and tampered traffic, forged signatures and tokens, recovered passwords, use of leaked credentials.
where: Clients (mobile apps, libraries, CLIs) that only partly validate certificates
Tokens generated from predictable sources
Signatures and JWTs where verification is optional or the algorithm can be swapped
Keys in repositories, apps and configuration files
test: Intercept with a proxy and see what the client accepts
Analyze token generation for patterns
Search repository history and binaries for secrets
fix: Current libraries and defaults; no home-made cryptography
Full validation of the certificate chain and name
A secrets manager, and rotation

categories.name: Security Misconfiguration
categories.blurb: CORS, headers, email, buckets and defaults left open.
categories.what: The software is correct but was deployed insecurely: permissive CORS, missing SPF/DMARC, public buckets, exposed panels, default credentials, absent security headers.
categories.impact: Depends on what is exposed. Many of these are closed as informative; the ones that pay give access to data or let someone impersonate the company.
where: CORS policies that reflect the origin with credentials
Cloud storage and IAM permissions
The domain's email records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
Admin panels and internal services exposed to the internet
test: Prove impact: a missing header alone is rarely accepted
For CORS, show authenticated data being read from another origin
For buckets, test listing and writing, not just reading
fix: Configuration as code, reviewed, with secure defaults
Continuous scanning of the exposed surface

categories.name: Other Injections
categories.blurb: HTML, CSV, LDAP, email and other interpreters.
categories.what: The same principle as SQLi and XSS, aimed elsewhere: HTML without script, formulas in exported spreadsheets, LDAP filters, email headers, arguments and resources.
categories.impact: Usually lower than the classic injections, but useful as a link in a chain: phishing through legitimate email, exfiltration through CSS, execution on the machine of whoever opens the spreadsheet.
where: Transactional emails carrying user-supplied fields
CSV and Excel exports
Directory lookups (LDAP) and argument building
test: Identify the destination interpreter and its special characters
Show a realistic exploitation scenario
fix: Escaping specific to each destination
Prefix cells starting with =, +, - or @ in exports

categories.name: AI, LLMs & Agents
categories.blurb: Prompt injection and flaws in systems built on language models.
categories.what: Untrusted content reaches the model and changes its behavior, or the application trusts the model's output too much: direct and indirect prompt injection, over-privileged tools, data leaking between contexts.
categories.impact: Exfiltration of conversation and connector data, unauthorized actions taken by the agent, code execution when the output feeds tools.
where: Agents with access to tools, files, a browser or a terminal
External content the model reads: pages, emails, documents, issues
How the answer is rendered (Markdown links and images) as an exit channel
test: Map what the model reads and what it is able to do
Plant instructions in sources the user does not control
Show concrete impact: data exfiltrated or an action performed
fix: Treat model output as untrusted input
Human confirmation for sensitive actions, and least-privilege tools
Separate data from instructions and limit exit channels

categories.name: Design & Validation Flaws
categories.blurb: Insecure design decisions and incomplete validation.
categories.what: A broad category for problems in how a feature was designed, or in generic input validation, that do not fit a more specific class.
categories.impact: Very mixed. Read the most upvoted ones to see how each case was argued.
where: New and rarely used features
Trust assumptions between components
test: Question the premises of each feature
Read the documentation looking for what it promises and fails to deliver
fix: Threat modeling at the start of the project
Secure defaults and centralized validation

categories.name: Unclassified
categories.blurb: Reports with no weakness set whose title does not give the class away.
categories.what: Reports disclosed without a weakness, and with a title that matches none of the taxonomy rules. They tend to be old reports (from before the platform required a type) or very specific cases.
